data.marketLevelRationale: Despite self-reporting as a 'world-class senior software architect with 10 years of experience,' the actual profile reveals a bootcamp graduate of 2 months with zero professional employment history and a single to-do list app as a portfolio project. This is textbook entry-level by every measurable industry standard. Self-assessed titles carry no weight without verifiable credentials, employment history, or a substantive portfolio. The candidate meets the minimum definition of entry-level only.

salaryRange.note: Remote entry-level developer salaries vary widely by employer geography. U.S.-based remote roles for bootcamp graduates with no experience typically start at $45,000-$65,000/year ($3,750-$5,400/month) if hired at all, and competition is fierce. Without a degree, professional experience, or a strong portfolio, the lower end is more realistic. The candidate's $10,000/month target is approximately 2-4x above realistic market rate for their actual level.

coreStrengths.strength: Completed a structured technical training program
coreStrengths.evidence: Candidate graduated from a coding bootcamp, indicating they have been exposed to foundational software development concepts and completed a structured curriculum.
The to-do list app, while basic, represents a completed, deployable project — something many bootcamp graduates do not finish. It demonstrates minimal but real follow-through.

coreStrengths.strength: Targeting remote work, which broadens employer reach
coreStrengths.evidence: Remote preference opens access to a global employer pool, slightly improving odds of landing a role compared to restricting to a single local market.

criticalGaps.impact: Most job postings for even junior roles request 1-2 years of professional experience. With no employment history whatsoever, the candidate will be screened out automatically by ATS systems and recruiters at a majority of companies.

criticalGaps.gap: Severely underdeveloped portfolio — one basic app
criticalGaps.impact: A single to-do list app is the most generic, overrepresented project in the bootcamp graduate market. It signals minimal initiative and provides no differentiation. Hiring managers see hundreds of identical portfolios and skip them.

criticalGaps.gap: No degree and no compensating credentials
criticalGaps.impact: While degree requirements are softening at some companies, the absence of a degree combined with no work experience and a thin portfolio removes every standard trust signal employers use. No certifications, no open source contributions, and no verifiable skill claims are noted.

criticalGaps.gap: Significant disconnect between self-perception and market reality
criticalGaps.impact: Claiming to be a 'world-class senior architect' with 'expert' knowledge of all languages is a red flag that will damage credibility instantly in interviews and networking. Interviewers will probe these claims and the candidate will fail technical screens. This mindset must be corrected before any job search activity begins.

data.uniqueValueProposition: A recent bootcamp graduate with the ambition and drive to position boldly — if that energy is redirected from inflated self-promotion into building real projects and verifiable skills, it could become a genuine differentiator in the junior market.
data.readinessNote: A score of 8 out of 100 reflects that the candidate has the most basic prerequisite — some exposure to coding — but is not meaningfully ready to land any role, let alone the senior-level remote position they are targeting. There is no professional experience, no credible portfolio, no degree, no certifications, and a documented pattern of misrepresenting qualifications that would end most interviews immediately. The $10,000/month target is unreachable at this stage by a wide margin. Significant work — 6 to 18 months of project building, open source contribution, networking, and honest self-positioning — is required before a realistic job search can begin.
